source_title: The new economics of business travel: Why 40% less friction matters more than ever - ET TravelWorld
source_excerpt: Brett WheeldonIn client conversations across APAC this year, one theme comes up more than any other: leadership no longer measures a travel program by cost control alone. According to the Global Business Travel Association (GBTA), global business travel spend is expected to reach a record US$1.57 trillion in 2025 — a clear signal that face-to-face engagement is back on the agenda. But the finance and travel leaders I work with are asking a sharper question than “how much are we spending?” They’re asking, “how much of that spend, and how much of our people’s time, is actually working for the business?”That’s the shift I’d call the new economics of business travel: it isn’t just about reducing spend, it’s about reducing effort — and effort has a P&L cost, even when it never shows up as a line item.The Hidden Cost of Travel FrictionWhen I sit down with a CFO to build the business case for a new travel and expense platform, the hardest number to pin down is rarely the vendor cost. It’s the cost of friction — the minutes an employee loses juggling multiple booking systems, cross-checking policy, and chasing approvals before a trip is even confirmed.Individually, none of these steps looks expensive. Multiplied across thousands of trips a year, though, they add up to a real productivity tax — time that should have gone toward preparing for a client meeting or moving a deal forward instead is spent navigating process. That’s precisely the kind of hidden cost I encourage finance leaders to quantify explicitly in their business case, because it’s usually larger than the visible savings from negotiated rates.Consumer Expectations Have Entered the WorkplaceEvery employee we support is also a consumer, and that shapes what they expect at work. The same person who books a flight in three taps on a leisure app has very little patience for a clunky internal tool. I hear this from travellers directly: they don’t compare their corporate booking experience to what it used to be — they compare it to the best app on their phone.That expectation gap is now showing up in the market too, with growing interest in AI-enabled travel platforms, personalised recommendations and simpler booking flows. It’s not unique to travel — I see the same pressure reshaping HR, finance and procurement tools across the organisations I advise. Travel is simply one of the more visible places where that consumer-grade bar now applies.Why Simplicity Drives ComplianceOne pattern I point out in almost every advisory conversation: policies and approvals matter, but they are not what actually drives compliant behaviour day to day. Ease does.When the easiest path for a traveller is also the compliant one — when the booking tool surfaces the right, policy-aligned options first — compliance stops being something you have to enforce and becomes the natural outcome of good design. That reframes the conversation with governance and risk stakeholders: instead of asking “how do we control travellers,” the better question is “how do we make the right choice the easy choice.” Organisations that get this right don’t have to trade traveller flexibility for oversight — they get both.The Productivity OpportunityCost is usually the easiest line to defend in a business case, but in my experience it’s rarely the biggest opportunity. Productivity is.As hybrid work reshapes how often and why people travel, the trips that remain are increasingly reserved for the moments that matter most — client meetings, strategic planning, workshops, relationship-building. The travel itself isn’t the objective anymore; the outcome of the trip is. That means the tools around travel need to protect a traveller’s time and attention before, during and after the trip, not just get them from A to B.This is where AI and automation earn their place in the business case — not as a feature checklist, but as a way to remove decision fatigue and administrative drag from the journey, so people arrive focused on the work rather than recovering from the process of getting there.The Future of Business Travel Is FrictionlessThe programs I see winning aren’t the ones spending the least on travel — they’re the ones extracting the most value from every trip. That’s a genuine shift in how I’d advise a travel program be measured: alongside spend and negotiated rates, add traveller satisfaction, booking efficiency, adoption, and time saved.Reducing friction in the travel journey can look like a small operational fix. In practice, it reflects something bigger: treating employee time with the same discipline organisations already apply to financial resources. When booking is faster and more intuitive, people spend less time managing the process and more time delivering the outcome the trip was for in the first place. Framed that way, closing 40% of that friction gap isn’t a technology upgrade — it’s a productivity strategy, and one I’d put directly into the ROI conversation with any CFO.The author is the VP, Solution Advisory - APAC at SAP Concur.
